column2: This is kaeng khiao wan, Thai green curry. It first shows up in a Thai cookbook from 1926. The very first Thai cookbooks, from the early 1890s, mention other curries, but not this one.
column3: Kaeng khiao wan: first seen in a 1926 cookbook.
column4: แกงเขียวหวาน พบครั้งแรกในตำราปี 1926

column2: The green comes from fresh green chillies, which is unusual, because most other Thai curries use red chillies. Wan means sweet, but here it describes a soft, pale shade of green, not the taste.
column3: Green from fresh chillies. Wan means a pale green.
column4: เขียวจากพริกสด หวานคือสีเขียวอ่อน ไม่ใช่รส

column2: Use Thai green chillies or serrano peppers for heat, plus milder green chillies, like Korean green peppers or jalapeños, for more chilli flavour without too much heat. Wear gloves, and remove the seeds if you like it milder.
column3: Spicy plus mild green chillies. Deseed for less heat.
column4: พริกเผ็ดผสมพริกเผ็ดน้อย ไม่ทนเผ็ดเอาเมล็ดออก

column2: Toast coriander seeds and cumin seeds, then grind them into a fine powder with white peppercorns. A coffee grinder gets them really fine.
column3: Toast coriander and cumin. Grind with white pepper.
column4: คั่วเมล็ดผักชีกับยี่หร่า บดกับพริกไทยขาว

column2: For the herbs, use only the bottom half of the lemongrass, never dried or powdered. Fresh or frozen galangal is best. Add makrut lime zest, or the zest of half a lime, and coriander root.
column3: Lemongrass, galangal, makrut lime zest, coriander root.
column4: ตะไคร้ ข่า ผิวมะกรูด รากผักชี

column2: In a large stone mortar, pound the chillies with coarse salt first, then the herbs, then shallots, garlic and the dry spices. An immersion blender works too.
column3: Pound chillies with salt, then herbs, shallots, garlic.
column4: โขลกพริกกับเกลือ แล้วสมุนไพร หอมแดง กระเทียม

column2: Finish with fermented shrimp paste, called gapi. Pailin says it is always added to traditional Thai curry pastes. A few Thai basil leaves boost the green colour, while their aroma cooks away.
column3: Shrimp paste (gapi). Thai basil for colour.
column4: กะปิ และใบโหระพาเพิ่มสีเขียว

column2: Short on time? Store-bought paste is fine, and most Thai people buy it premade too. Most commercial pastes skip shrimp paste, so add a little. Brands vary hugely in strength, so taste as you go.
column3: Store-bought is fine. Add shrimp paste, then taste.
column4: พริกแกงสำเร็จก็ได้ เติมกะปิแล้วชิม

column2: Bring some coconut milk to a full boil, add the paste, and fry it, stirring often, until the coconut oil starts to separate. Those little green dots of oil show the paste has released its flavour.
column3: Fry the paste in coconut milk until the oil separates.
column4: ผัดพริกแกงกับกะทิจนน้ำมันแยกตัว

column2: Add chicken thigh, the most common choice and the tastiest, then the rest of the coconut milk, stock, fish sauce and palm sugar. Bruise the makrut lime leaves and tear them in.
column3: Chicken thigh, fish sauce, palm sugar, makrut lime leaves.
column4: ไก่สะโพก น้ำปลา น้ำตาลปี๊บ ใบมะกรูด

column2: Thai eggplant goes in next. Cook it until a fork goes through with slight resistance. No Thai eggplant? Canned bamboo shoots work; just give them a rinse.
column3: Thai eggplant, or canned bamboo shoots.
column4: มะเขือเปราะ หรือหน่อไม้กระป๋อง

column2: Stir in Thai basil just until it wilts. Taste, and add more fish sauce if needed. It should be spicy and salty, with only a lick of sweetness from the coconut. Serve with jasmine rice.
column3: Thai basil. Spicy and salty, not sweet.
column4: ใส่โหระพา รสเผ็ดเค็ม ไม่หวาน

column3: In Thailand? Links are in the caption.
